faqs.q: How can I tell if my East Orange building has wind damage after a storm?

runs.v: Lifted, creased, or torn shingle tabs, peeled ridge and hip caps, and bent or missing flashing at edges and dormers are the first signs of wind damage, and they appear first at the corners, rakes, and edges, where wind uplift concentrates, per IIBEC. On flat roofs, check parapet caps and edge metal for gaps; asphalt grit, torn tabs, or debris in the yard after a 58 mph gust indicates severe-storm wind loading, per NOAA.

faqs.q: Do wind-lifted shingles that settled back down count as damaged?

runs.v: Yes, if the seal broke: the seal between shingle courses governs wind resistance, so a broken seal leaves no resistance to the next gust. The seal strength ranks as the most important high-wind factor, per IBHS wind-uplift research, so a Newark Quality Roofing inspection tests seals by hand across the field rather than judging the roof on appearance alone.

faqs.q: Does insurance cover wind damage on my East Orange rental property roof?

runs.v: Wind is a covered peril under a standard New Jersey homeowners and landlord policy, with the all-perils deductible applying to a wind claim, per the NJ Department of Banking and Insurance. The deciding factor is documenting that the damage is wind-caused, not wear-related, and filing promptly strengthens the claim because physical evidence degrades over time.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit from East Orange for wind damage roof repair?

runs.v: A repair or replacement of the roof covering on a detached one- or two-family home counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit, inspection, or notice to the construction official. On a commercial, multi-family, or attached building, repairing more than 25% of the total roof area in a 12-month period requires a permit, a path that applies often in East Orange's heavily multi-family stock.

faqs.q: Can wind damage on one East Orange building affect an adjacent property?

runs.v: Yes. Shingles, flashing, and other materials blown from one roof can damage adjacent structures, and on East Orange's narrow multi-family blocks wind-borne debris frequently strikes a neighboring building's siding, windows, or roof. When secondary damage comes from materials originating next door, the responsible party's insurance typically covers it, so a Newark Quality Roofing wind assessment documents the origin of debris.
